Placebo effect works in video games too

In the first round, the researchers told the players that the map would be randomly generated. In the second, they said it would be controlled by an “adaptive AI” that could change the map based on the player’s skill level. After each round, the players filled out a survey.

In fact, neither game used AI – both versions of the game were identically random.

This seems flawed to me. When subjects were told the 2nd map would be based on their skill level, they had no idea what to expect, since they had only played a single game. What is a "hard" game? What is an "easy" game? If the subjects don't know what to expect, it may as well have been exactly the same as using a real "adaptive AI." Basically, any change in game experience could be interpreted as the intention of the AI. You need to have people play multiple games beforehand to make this a reliable test.

Did I explain that well? Does anyone have any thoughts on this?

Edit: Furthermore, a 2nd game might be naturally more enjoyable, since they had some time to get familiar with the game. Also, this doesn't really apply to the 2nd experiment, but they didn't give many details about that one, so I'm not trying to judge it.

"The adaptive AI put me in a safer environment and seemed to present me with resources as needed,” said one player.

“It reduces the time of exploring the map, which makes the game more enjoyable,” said another."

Either way, the play testers thought an A.I. was partially catering to fit their skill level.
Yes, but the randomness of the level may have actually produced the changes that the players perceived. They have no baseline to anchor them to the experience of a "normal" game.

Not gonna lie, this has happened to me. Especially in COD AW, some guns that say they do more damage actually do the same damage but have different environmental penetration values. Mobility also does not translate to move speed. When I picked up a gun with higher mobility and damage it felt like it killed faster and was faster, until I did enough research to see what the figures actually meant.

I still don't see how using a RNG based game is any baseline for a placebo effect... the experiences between games will change drastically. Anyone that has gotten a rare drop on the first try will think a game is hella EZ.

So basically players have trouble discerning between random map design and adaptive map design over two games. Not to mention that in Don't Starve, it would be difficult to characterize both player skill and the difficulty of a map.
